questions.question: Choose the most efficient test for the series below.

moves.name: Limit Comparison Test with 1/n
moves.professor: The dominant term ratio is 1/n. One Limit Comparison and you've cornered the divergence.

moves.name: Direct Comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: That inequality points the wrong direction—1/n^2 is smaller, you proved nothing.

moves.name: Integral Test
moves.professor: It's doable, but you're bringing heavy machinery to a duel. Limit comparison is the rapier.

moves.name: Divergence Test, limit is 1 ≠ 0
moves.professor: Check again—the terms approach 0. The Divergence Test is silent here.

questions.question: What is the best way to determine convergence of the improper integral below?

moves.name: Recognize it as a convergent arctan integral
moves.professor: Classic arctan form. Converges to π/4—elegant, no splitting needed.

moves.name: Split at 0 because the integrand is undefined at 0
moves.professor: The integrand is 1/4 at x=0, perfectly well-behaved. Don't create imaginary wounds.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^2
moves.professor: Comparison works, but it's the long way round. Recognize the arctan and finish in one stroke.

questions.question: Find the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: e^3, by recognizing the exponential form
moves.professor: A direct hit on the definition of e^c. The pattern is unmistakable.

moves.name: 1, because 1+3/n approaches 1 and 1^n = 1
moves.professor: 1^∞ is a decoy. You walked right into the indeterminate form ambush.

moves.name: Take logarithm and apply L'Hôpital's Rule
moves.professor: Solid backup tactic. It confirms e^3, but recognition would have been faster.

questions.question: Classify the convergence type of the alternating series below.

moves.name: Conditionally convergent; AST applies, p=1/2 diverges
moves.professor: Alternating signs tame the slow decay. Conditional convergence—exactly right.

moves.name: Absolutely convergent by p-series
moves.professor: Absolute value gives the harmonic p=1/2 series—that diverges. No absolute shield here.

moves.name: Diverges because terms do not approach 0
moves.professor: 1/√n vanishes, so the divergence test is useless. The series does converge, conditionally.

moves.name: Ratio Test shows absolute convergence
moves.professor: Ratio Test here yields 1—inconclusive. You dodged a wrong answer, but didn't strike.

questions.question: Decide the best method for the series below.

moves.name: Integral Test; ∫ dx/(x(ln x)^2) converges
moves.professor: The Integral Test was born for this form. Converges cleanly.

moves.name: Comparison with 1/n, series diverges
moves.professor: The series is smaller than the harmonic series—you can't conclude divergence from that.

moves.name: Limit Comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: Limit goes to 0, which doesn't directly tell you convergence. Integral Test is the sharper weapon.

questions.question: Evaluate the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: Multiply by conjugate; limit is 1
moves.professor: Conjugate attack clears the radical. The hidden 1 emerges.

moves.name: Limit is 0 because the two terms cancel at infinity
moves.professor: ∞−∞ is not zero. It's a trap you must dismantle with algebra.

moves.name: Factor out n and use Taylor expansion
moves.professor: Works, but the conjugate move is cleaner. Still, you landed the correct limit.

questions.question: Choose a comparison to establish convergence of the improper integral.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^2 for large x
moves.professor: For large x, √(x²-4) ~ x, so the integrand behaves like 1/x². That seals it.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x; the integral diverges
moves.professor: 1/x is too big; the actual function is smaller so the comparison is inconclusive.

moves.name: Use trig substitution x=2 sec θ
moves.professor: Leads to an answer, but why unsheathe a greatsword when a comparison dagger finishes the job?

questions.question: Determine the convergence of the series using optimal test.

moves.name: Ratio Test; limit is 1/e < 1, converges
moves.professor: Factorial vs power? Ratio Test slices through it instantly.

moves.name: Divergence Test; terms do not go to 0
moves.professor: The terms approach 0. You misjudged their decay. Divergence Test won't fire.

moves.name: Root Test
moves.professor: Also effective, but Ratio Test is usually the first blade drawn for factorials.

questions.question: Find the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: 1; use logarithm, limit is 0
moves.professor: The nth root of n creeps toward 1. Logarithm reveals the truth.

moves.name: 0 because the exponent 1/n drives it to 0
moves.professor: Base n grows while exponent shrinks—0 is not their compromise. Wrong instinct.

moves.name: Infinity; n dominates any root
moves.professor: Even the mighty n is humbled by its own nth root. It tends to 1.

questions.question: Identify the quickest convergence test for the series.

moves.name: Ratio Test; limit = 1/2 < 1
moves.professor: Ratio Test dispatches geometric-exponential mixes in one move.

moves.name: Integral Test with integration by parts
moves.professor: You're hacking through the jungle when a trail is clearly marked. Too cumbersome.

moves.name: Direct Comparison with 1/2^n
moves.professor: You can compare, but setting up the inequality takes more effort than Ratio Test.

questions.question: Determine the convergence type of the series.

moves.name: Absolutely convergent by comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: |cos n| ≤ 1, so the series is dominated by a convergent p-series. Absolute victory.

moves.name: Diverges because cosine oscillates
moves.professor: Oscillation doesn't imply divergence if the amplitude shrinks fast enough. Here it's tamed.

moves.name: Conditionally convergent by Alternating Series Test
moves.professor: The signs aren't strictly alternating. AST doesn't apply; the series is actually absolutely convergent.

questions.question: Determine if the series converges and, if so, find its sum.

moves.name: Telescoping series; sum = 1/2
moves.professor: Telescope collapses instantly—first minus last remaining term. Sum is 1/2.

moves.name: Diverges by Integral Test
moves.professor: The terms telescope, not diverge. You applied the wrong strategy entirely.

moves.name: Converges to 1 by geometric series formula
moves.professor: This isn't geometric. Missing the telescoping nature cost you.

questions.question: Which method best confirms convergence of the improper integral?

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^{5/2} for large x
moves.professor: ln x grows slower than any power, so x^{5/2} in denominator dominates. Converges.

moves.name: Integration by parts
moves.professor: You'll get the exact value, but comparison is a faster kill.

moves.name: The integral diverges because ln x → ∞
moves.professor: x^3 in the denominator crushes ln x. Divergence is a false alarm.

questions.question: Find the radius of convergence of the power series.

moves.name: Radius = 1 by Ratio Test
moves.professor: The boundary is at |x|=1. Ratio Test yields the radius cleanly.

moves.name: Radius = ∞; the terms decay factorially
moves.professor: No factorial here, and the n in the denominator doesn't grant infinite radius.

moves.name: Radius = 0
moves.professor: The series certainly converges for x=0, but the radius is positive. Check again.

questions.question: Evaluate the limit.

moves.name: L'Hôpital's Rule; limit is 1
moves.professor: 0/0 form. One round of L'Hôpital fells it—derivative of numerator at 0 is 1.

moves.name: Plug in x=0 directly; limit is 0/0 undefined so DNE
moves.professor: 0/0 is an invitation to fight, not an excuse to retreat. Apply L'Hôpital or series.

moves.name: Use series expansions up to x
moves.professor: Series also leads to 1; thorough, though L'Hôpital is quicker here.

questions.question: Determine why the series diverges.

moves.name: Divergence Test; terms oscillate and limit ≠ 0
moves.professor: The terms swing between values near 1 and -1. No approach to 0 means instant divergence.

moves.name: Use Alternating Series Test; it diverges by AST
moves.professor: AST requires terms to go to 0. They don't. The test doesn't even apply.

moves.name: Use Ratio Test; limit = 1 so diverges
moves.professor: Ratio Test gives 1—inconclusive, not divergence. You're left empty-handed.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate test for the series.

moves.name: Integral Test with u = x^2; converges
moves.professor: The continuous version yields an easy u-sub. Converges rapidly.

moves.name: Diverges because the terms do not approach 0
moves.professor: n e^{-n^2} plummets to 0 faster than you think. Divergence Test is useless here.

moves.name: Ratio Test
moves.professor: Ratio Test works (limit 0) but is slightly more involved. Integral Test is more direct.

questions.question: Find the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: 1, using lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1
moves.professor: Substitute x = 1/n and the fundamental limit does all the work. Clean.

moves.name: 0, because sin(1/n) → 0
moves.professor: n battles the small sine—the product tends to 1, not 0. Classic growth-rate trap.

moves.name: Apply L'Hôpital's Rule after rewriting
moves.professor: Valid but heavier. Recognition of the sin x / x limit is the faster blade.

questions.question: Determine convergence or divergence of the improper integral.

moves.name: Converges to -1; limit comparison or direct evaluation
moves.professor: Despite the vertical asymptote, the area is finite. -1 is the calm result.

moves.name: Diverges because ln x → -∞ as x→0+
moves.professor: A blow-up doesn't guarantee infinite area—the spike is integrable. Common overreaction.

moves.name: Use the p-integral rule with p=0
moves.professor: ln x is not a power function. The p-test rules don't apply here. You sidestepped, but didn't solve.

questions.question: Choose the best test for the series.

moves.name: Integral Test; ∫ 1/(x^2+1) dx converges
moves.professor: Positive, continuous, decreasing—Integral Test grants a quick convergence verdict.

moves.name: Divergence Test; terms go to 0 so diverges
moves.professor: Vanishing terms are the minimum requirement, not a sign of divergence. Check your logic.

moves.name: Comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: Also works perfectly. Either route leads to convergence. Take your pick.
